title: Work & study
goal: Talk about jobs, school and university, and say what you can, can't, must and have to do.
intro:
Education is highly valued in Pashtun society — 'the pen is the light of the eye' — and you'll meet teachers, students, farmers, shopkeepers, drivers and traders in every village. Many Pashtun men also work far from home, in Karachi, the Gulf or Europe, sending money back to their families.

In this unit you'll learn words for jobs and study, how to say **can** with the special Pashto 'potential' form (ويلای شم 'I can say'), and **must / have to** with بايد and مجبور.

vocab.note: m · pl: ښوونکي. f: ښوونکې ṣowúnke. Also استاد ustā́z.
m. f: زده کوونکې. Also محصل 'university student'.
The potential form of کول; see grammar.
f. مجبوره. مجبور يم چې … 'I have to …'.

phrases.native: زه په پوهنتون کې درس وايم.
phrases.roman: zə pə pohantún ke dars wā́yəm.

phrases.native: زه مجبور يم چې سبا هم کار وکړم.
phrases.roman: zə majbúr yəm che sabā́ ham kār wə́kṛəm.
phrases.en: I have to work tomorrow too.

phrases.native: سبا ازموينه لرم، بايد درس ووايم.
phrases.roman: sabā́ azmóyəna lárəm, bāyád dars wə́wāyəm.
phrases.en: I have an exam tomorrow, I must study.
What time does your office open?

grammar.title: 'Can': the potential form (ويلای شم)
grammar.body:
Pashto says 'can' with a special **potential** form: the infinitive + **-āy** (ـای), followed by the perfective of 'become', **شم** (shəm), which takes the person endings:

ليکل → **ليکلای شم** 'I can write'
ويل → **ويلای شې** 'you can say'
تلل → **تللای شي** 'he can go'
راتلل → **راتلای شو** 'we can come'
کول → **کولای شئ** 'you (pl.) can do'

In the **negative**, نه goes before شم and the two parts swap round: زه **نه شم** ليکلای 'I can't write'. (Some speakers keep the order: نه ليکلای شم.)

You will also hear **کولای شم چې** + subjunctive: کولای شم چې درسره مرسته وکړم 'I can help you'. In Pakistan and in casual speech the spelling ـلی is common: ويلی شم.

examples.native: تاسو کولای شئ چې دلته کار وکړئ.
examples.roman: tāso kawə́lāy shəy che dálta kār wə́kṛəy.

grammar.title: 'Must' and 'have to': بايد and مجبور
grammar.body:
**بايد** + subjunctive (perfective present) is the general 'must / should' (unit 9): بايد لاړ شم 'I must go'.

**مجبور يم چې** + subjunctive means 'I'm obliged to / I have to' (outside pressure): مجبور يم چې دا کار وکړم 'I have no choice but to do this'. مجبور agrees with the subject: مجبوره يم (woman).

Other useful expressions:
**اړ يم چې …** 'I need to …' (اړ 'in need')
**ضرور** 'certainly, definitely': ضرور به راشم 'I'll definitely come'
**پکار نه دی** 'it's not necessary': دا کار پکار نه دی 'there's no need for this'.

For 'don't have to', say **ضرورت نشته چې** 'there's no need that': ضرورت نشته چې سبا راشې 'you don't have to come tomorrow'.

examples.native: زه بايد اته بجې دفتر ته لاړ شم.
examples.roman: zə bāyád atə́ báje daftár ta lāṛ shəm.
examples.en: I must go to the office at eight.

examples.native: هغه مجبوره ده چې کور کې پاتې شي.
examples.roman: haġá majbúra da che kor ke pā́te shi.
examples.en: She has to stay at home.

examples.native: موږ اړ يو چې پيسې وګټو.
examples.roman: muẓ aṛ yu che páyse wə́gaṭu.

examples.en: You don't have to come tomorrow.

examples.native: شاګردان بايد هره ورځ درس ووايي.
examples.roman: shāgərdā́n bāyád hára wradz dars wə́wāyi.

dialogue.title: A job interview
dialogue.setting: Roshan applies for an office job at an organisation in Kabul. The director interviews her.

lines.speaker: Director
lines.native: ښه راغلې. ته اوس څه کار کوې؟
lines.roman: ṣə rā́ġle. tə os tsə kār kawé?
lines.en: Welcome. What do you do at the moment?

lines.speaker: Roshan
lines.native: زه په يوه ښوونځي کې ښوونکې يم، خو نوې دنده لټوم.
lines.roman: zə pə yáwa ṣowundzí ke ṣowúnke yəm, xo náwe dánda laṭawə́m.
lines.en: I'm a teacher at a school, but I'm looking for a new job.

lines.speaker: Director
lines.native: چېرته دې زده کړه کړې ده؟
lines.en: Where did you get your education?

lines.speaker: Roshan
lines.native: د کابل په پوهنتون کې. درې کاله تجربه هم لرم.
lines.roman: də kābúl pə pohantún ke. dre kā́la tajrubá ham lárəm.
lines.en: At Kabul University. I also have three years' experience.

lines.speaker: Director
lines.native: انګرېزي ويلای شې؟ په کمپيوټر کار کولای شې؟
lines.roman: angrezí wayə́lāy she? pə kampyuṭár kār kawə́lāy she?
lines.en: Can you speak English? Can you work on a computer?

lines.speaker: Roshan
lines.native: هو، دواړه کولای شم. انګرېزي لوستلای او ليکلای شم.
lines.roman: ho, dwā́ṛa kawə́lāy shəm. angrezí lwastə́lāy aw likə́lāy shəm.
lines.en: Yes, I can do both. I can read and write English.

lines.speaker: Director
lines.native: ښه. دلته بايد له شنبې نه تر پنجشنبې پورې کار وکړې.
lines.roman: ṣə. dálta bāyád la shanbé na tər panjshanbé póre kār wə́kṛe.
lines.en: Good. Here you'd have to work from Saturday to Thursday.

lines.speaker: Roshan
lines.native: سمه ده. خو د پنجشنبې ماسپښين نه شم پاتې کېدای.
lines.roman: sáma da. xo də panjshanbé māspṣín na shəm pā́te kedā́y.
lines.en: That's fine. But I can't stay on Thursday afternoons.

lines.speaker: Director
lines.native: کومه ستونزه نشته. سبا به درته زنګ ووهو.
lines.roman: kúma stúnza nə́shta. sabā́ ba dərta zang wə́wahu.
lines.en: No problem. We'll call you tomorrow.

culture: Teachers (استاد، ښوونکی) are deeply respected, and you'll hear students greet them with استاد جان or استاد صاحب. Many families make great sacrifices to send their children to school and university, and Pashtun women have long campaigned for education — Malala Yousafzai from Swat is the world's best-known example. Farming, trade and transport are traditional Pashtun occupations, and Pashtun truckers and traders run much of the long-distance trade between Pakistan and Afghanistan. Asking someone's profession is a normal part of getting to know them.
